title: Essays on Art and Science
description:
Seven essays in which a Nobel-winning neuroscientist applies brain science to how viewers perceive and feel about painting and sculpture.

Eric Kandel explains our emotional responses to art through unconscious processes of perception, memory and emotion. He starts from Vienna 1900 and the exchange between Christians and Jews that produced Viennese modernism. He returns to the beholder's share, the idea that a viewer completes an artwork. Other essays treat Chaim Soutine, the modern representation of women, portraiture, Cubism, sculpture against painting, and abstract against figurative art. Columbia University Press published the hardcover in March 2024.

Kandel shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his studies of learning and memory and is University Professor Emeritus at Columbia. His earlier books on art and the mind include The Age of Insight (2012) and Reductionism in Art and Brain Science (Columbia, 2016).

title: Stealing the Mona Lisa: What Art Stops Us from Seeing
description:
A psychoanalyst's essay on why famous paintings are looked at less than they are visited, built around the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa from the Louvre.

Leader starts from the crowds who came to see the empty space where the painting had hung, many of whom had never seen it. From there he asks what viewers want from a painting, why artists sometimes live more dramatically than their work suggests, and why investigators struggled with the case. He combines anecdote and observation with analysis of classical and contemporary works. The Counterpoint hardcover is the American first edition; a Faber and Faber edition appeared in Britain.

Darian Leader (b. 1965) is a British psychoanalyst associated with the Lacanian tradition and a founding member of the Centre for Freudian Analysis and Research in London. His other books include Freud's Footnotes (2000), The New Black (2008) and Why Can't We Sleep? (2019).

title: Distinguishing Piss from Rain: Writings and Interviews
description:
The collected writings and interviews of Glenn Ligon, gathered across more than twenty years of a practice built on text and on Black literary voices.

The volume brings together essays and interviews from the early 2000s onward, edited by James Hoff with an introduction by T. Jean Lax. Ligon writes on contemporary and historical artists, among them Philip Guston, David Hammons and Andy Warhol, and the book places Black identity at the centre of art institutions that have mostly been white. It runs to about 400 pages with 80 colour and 20 black-and-white reproductions, and was published by Hauser & Wirth Publishers in 2024.

Glenn Ligon was born in the Bronx in 1960 and moved from abstract painting to text-based paintings, installations and neons. His work repeatedly quotes James Baldwin, Zora Neale Hurston and other Black writers. It is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Baltimore Museum of Art.

title: Weight of the Earth: The Tape Journals of David Wojnarowicz
description:
The transcribed tape journals of David Wojnarowicz, recorded as he faced an AIDS diagnosis and the loss of friends in late-1980s New York.

The tapes were made mainly in 1987 and 1989, on solitary road trips and in his New York loft. They cover his frustration with the art world, his dreams, his reaction to his HIV diagnosis, and his thoughts on death, sexuality, violence and the limits of language. Lisa Darms and David O'Neill edited the transcripts and David Velasco wrote the introduction. The recordings are held at the Fales Library at New York University.

David Wojnarowicz (1954-1992) was a painter, photographer, filmmaker, performer and writer. He was in the 1985 Whitney Biennial and made the film A Fire in My Belly (1986-1987). His memoirs include Close to the Knives (1991) and Memories That Smell Like Gasoline (1992).

title: Let's Have a Talk: Conversations with Women on Art and Culture
description:
A collection of over 80 interviews with women in art, music and writing, drawn from thirteen years of Lauren O'Neill-Butler's work as an interviewer and editor.

Most of the conversations first ran in the interviews column on Artforum.com, which she edited for eleven years. The book has two parts: "Q&A", in conventional question-and-answer form, and "As Told To", where she recasts the conversation in the interviewee's own voice. The subjects include Judy Chicago, Yoko Ono, Carolee Schneemann, Nan Goldin, Sophie Calle, Joan Jonas and Donna J. Haraway. Karma published it in New York in a 456-page paperback.

O'Neill-Butler is a writer and educator and a co-founder of the magazine November. The book gathers the interviewing that formed much of her career at Artforum.

title: Autobiography
description:
The late memoir of the German-Australian photographer Helmut Newton (1920-2004), published in English in 2003, the year before his death.

Newton traces his life from Berlin under the Nazis, through his years in Australia, to a career as an internationally known fashion and portrait photographer. The book is illustrated with photographs. It first appeared in German in 2002 as Autobiographie from C. Bertelsmann, Munich, and this is the Nan A. Talese/Doubleday edition for the American market.

Newton's photographs for Vogue and other magazines, with their erotically charged black-and-white imagery, were collected in books such as White Women (1976), Sleepless Nights (1978), World Without Men (1984) and Sumo (1999). The Autobiography is his own account of the life behind them, and it appeared just months before his death.

title: Painting Below Zero: Notes on a Life in Art
description:
The Pop artist James Rosenquist (1933-2017) tells his life story in his own voice, written with David Dalton and published by Knopf in 2009.

The memoir starts in the farming communities of North Dakota and Minnesota where Rosenquist grew up, and follows him to Broadway scaffolds as a sign painter and to the artists' circle at Coenties Slip in New York. He recalls studying with George Grosz, his friendships with Willem de Kooning, Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns, a serious car accident in 1971, and his advocacy for artists' rights. He also discusses the thinking behind paintings such as Zone, F-111 and Star Thief.

Rosenquist worked as a billboard painter from 1957 to 1960 and brought that scale and technique into fine art. F-111 (1964-65), roughly 26 meters long, is the best known of his room-size paintings. This book is the artist's own account of how those pictures came to be made.

description:
An anthology on love edited by Ingo Niermann, the ninth volume of Sternberg Press's Solution series.

Where earlier volumes took up geopolitical questions, this one treats love through biopolitical and psychosexual lenses. Contributions range from manifestos to speculative fiction and consider love as a mix of charity, sex, trust, lust, economics, genetics and cybernetics, with embodiment and identity understood as fluid systems with permeable boundaries. The book has 188 pages and 18 black-and-white illustrations.

Contributors include Etel Adnan, Douglas Coupland, Eva Illouz, Ben Marcus, Chus Martínez, Momus, Paul B. Preciado and Emily Segal, alongside Niermann himself. The publisher lists the volume as out of print.

title: Rich Texts: Selected Writing for Art
description:
A collection of critical essays by the artist and writer John Kelsey, published by Sternberg Press in 2010 in its Institut für Kunstkritik series.

The book gathers Kelsey's writing from the preceding decade, much of it first printed in Artforum, Texte zur Kunst, Parkett and artists' catalogues. It is edited by Daniel Birnbaum and Isabelle Graw, who describe texts that are playful and true to the situations they observe. The essays work from inside the commercial art world and ask how criticism can drop its traditional distance from its subject.

Kelsey is an American artist and writer, a member of the collective Bernadette Corporation since 1999 and, with Emily Sundblad, a co-founder in 2004 of the gallery Reena Spaulings Fine Art. The book is a selection of that work.

title: Where Art Belongs
description:
Four essays by the writer and filmmaker Chris Kraus on art made from lived time. She argues the art world is still a place to try living differently.

The book moves from New York to Berlin to Los Angeles to the Pueblo Nuevo barrio of Mexicali. Its subjects include the ubiquity of video, the 1960s Amsterdam underground newspaper Suck and the New York collective Bernadette Corporation. Kraus also covers boredom, poetry, privatized prisons, community art and corporate philanthropy. Her thread is small groups reclaiming public space and time.

Kraus extends the argument of her earlier book Video Green, that the art world is interesting only insofar as it reflects the larger world outside it. Where Art Belongs appeared in January 2011 as number 8 in the Semiotext(e) Intervention series.

title: The Space of Agonism: Markus Miessen in Conversation with Chantal Mouffe
description:
Conversations between the architect Markus Miessen and the political theorist Chantal Mouffe on agonism, the idea that democratic space depends on conflict as well as consensus.

The dialogues date from 2006 to 2011 and take up conflict-based forms of participation as an alternative spatial practice, Mouffe's concept of conflictual consensus, and strategies for resisting the global spread of neoliberalism. The book includes 23 colour illustrations and artwork and text by Rabih Mroue, and was designed by Zak Group. Parts 1 to 3 were published earlier in Miessen's The Nightmare of Participation.

Miessen (b. Bonn, 1978) is a German architect and writer who edits the Critical Spatial Practice series with Nikolaus Hirsch. Mouffe (b. 1943) is a Belgian political theorist known for her work with Ernesto Laclau and for arguing for a conflict-oriented model of radical democracy. Sternberg Press published the book in Berlin in 2012.

title: Caravaggio: Painter of Miracles
description:
A short biography of the painter Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571-1610), written by the novelist and critic Francine Prose rather than by an art historian.

Prose follows Caravaggio from the most sought-after painter in Rome to a fugitive accused of murder, and sets his brawls, scandals and duels against the religious paintings he made in the same years. Her attention goes to the pictures: she reads each as a moment of theatrical revelation and dwells on his use of street boys, prostitutes, the poor and the aged as models for sacred scenes. Publishers Weekly called the result an informal appreciation more than a full biography. It was published in 2005 by Atlas Books and HarperCollins in the Eminent Lives series.

Prose is an American novelist, short story writer, essayist and critic, writer-in-residence at Bard College and a former president of PEN American Center. Other volumes in Eminent Lives pair writers with their subjects, among them Bill Bryson on Shakespeare and Christopher Hitchens on Jefferson.

title: Hold Still: A Memoir with Photographs
description:
A memoir by the photographer Sally Mann that combines her own account of her youth and family with photographs, and asks how photography shapes a view of the world.

Published by Little, Brown in May 2015, the book joins memoir with an examination of some of the major influences on Mann's life. It grew out of a lecture she gave and runs to 482 pages with illustrations, some in colour. It was a finalist for the 2015 National Book Award and won the 2016 Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence in Nonfiction. The race and slavery history of the American South that runs through it has become central to her later projects.

Mann (b. 1951) is an American photographer known for large-format black-and-white pictures of her children, her husband, the rural landscape around her and herself. Hold Still is her ninth book. The Getty record lists this hardcover as a first edition.

title: Great Demon Kings: A Memoir of Poetry, Sex, Art, Death, and Enlightenment
description:
A posthumous memoir by the New York poet and performer John Giorno (1936-2019), written as an account of his life in poetry, sex, art, death and Buddhist practice.

The memoir is a run of lovers, teachers and friends. Giorno recounts his relationship with Andy Warhol, which began when he appeared in Warhol's 1964 film Sleep, and affairs with Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns, the latter during the years of Dial-A-Poem. William Burroughs and Allen Ginsberg recur throughout, Ginsberg turning up even on Giorno's trip to India in search of enlightenment. The book also covers his Tibetan Buddhist practice, his place among the Beats and the New York avant-garde, and the AIDS Treatment Project he founded in 1984. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published it in 2020. Kirkus Reviews called it upbeat, funny and unsparing.

Giorno founded Giorno Poetry Systems in 1965 to present poetry through recordings, performances and other media, and in 1969 he started the telephone project Dial-A-Poem. He was married to the artist Ugo Rondinone. This memoir is the fullest account of that career in his own words.

title: Duty Free Art: Art in the Age of Planetary Civil War
description:
A collection of essays in which Hito Steyerl asks how art can be made or appreciated when arms manufacturers sponsor museums and valuable artworks serve as a currency in speculative markets.

The essays take up video games, WikiLeaks, spam and the circulation of images, and treat the contemporary art world as part of the political economy it appears to comment on. Verso published the collection in 2017 as Duty Free Art, with a paperback following in 2019.

Steyerl (b. 1966, Munich) is a filmmaker and writer who has taught new media art at the Berlin University of the Arts. Her video works include How Not To Be Seen: A Fucking Didactic Educational .MOV File (2013) and Factory of the Sun (2015). Her essays and her moving-image work address the same subjects: media, technology, militarization and the global circulation of images.

title: Death and Disaster: The Rise of the Warhol Empire and the Race for Andy's Millions
description:
A journalist's account of the fight over Andy Warhol's legacy after his death in 1987, when his estate, his foundation and his lawyer ended up in court over what his work and holdings were worth.

Warhol died within a day of routine gallbladder surgery. The book follows what came next. His townhouse was sealed and canvases were moved to a warehouse. The estate held furniture, jewelry, real estate, a magazine and a large store of his own unsold work. Estimates of its value ranged widely, and in April 1994 a New York surrogate's court judge fixed it at more than half a billion dollars. Villard published the book in 1994, with 258 pages and 16 pages of plates.

Alexander is an American journalist and biographer. His other books include Boulevard of Broken Dreams, on James Dean, and the biographies Rough Magic (Sylvia Plath) and Salinger.

title: The Bride and the Bachelors
description:
Calvin Tomkins's account of five artists who pursued what Robert Rauschenberg called the gap between art and life. It was first published in 1965 and appears here in a revised edition.

The chapters treat Marcel Duchamp, John Cage, Jean Tinguely, Robert Rauschenberg and Merce Cunningham, drawing on interviews and first-hand contact with the artists. This edition adds new material on Jasper Johns and a preface by the author. It is a 484-page cloth hardcover in a dust jacket, published by Gagosian, which lists it as 2014.

Tomkins (1925-2026) joined The New Yorker as a staff writer in 1960 and served as its art critic from 1980 to 1986. His other books include Off the Wall: A Portrait of Robert Rauschenberg (1980), Duchamp: A Biography (1996) and Lives of the Artists (2008).

title: Walk Through Walls: A Memoir
description:
A memoir in which the performance artist Marina Abramović, written with James Kaplan, recounts her life from childhood in postwar Yugoslavia to her international career.

The book follows her upbringing under Tito's regime as the child of Communist war-hero parents, her early performances, and the twelve-year collaboration with the artist Ulay that ended on the Great Wall of China. It reaches her 2010 retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, where more than 750,000 people queued to sit across from her in a durational piece. Crown Archetype published it in October 2016, and Booklist and Publishers Weekly both gave it starred reviews.

Abramović is known for performances that push the body and emotions to their limits. The memoir is her own account of the life behind that work. She divides her time between New York and the Hudson Valley.

title: Diane Arbus: Portrait of a Photographer
description:
A biography of the photographer Diane Arbus by Arthur Lubow that ties the course of her life to the photographs that made her name.

Lubow follows Arbus from a wealthy New York childhood through her years as a successful fashion photographer to the work in which she drew secrets out of her subjects. He draws on interviews with her friends, lovers and colleagues and on previously unknown letters. The book runs to roughly 730 pages. Ecco, an imprint of HarperCollins, published it in 2016, and Publishers Weekly gave it a starred review.

Arthur Lubow, born in 1952, is an American journalist who graduated from Harvard in 1974 and has written for The New Yorker, Vanity Fair and The New York Times Magazine. The book grew out of his cover story on Arbus for the Times Magazine in September 2003, and by his own account he spent twelve years on research and reporting. It follows Patricia Bosworth's 1984 biography and runs to more than twice its length. Lubow adds material from her psychotherapy conversations that Bosworth did not publish.

title: Frank Auerbach: Speaking and Painting
description:
A study of the painter Frank Auerbach built from the artist's own words, assembled by the curator Catherine Lampert from nearly four decades of conversations.

Lampert has known Auerbach since 1978, when she became one of his sitters, and she combines her talks with him with published and archival interviews. The book covers his working methods and philosophy, his arrival in Britain in 1939 as a child refugee from Nazi Germany, and his friendships with Leon Kossoff, Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud. It has about 100 illustrations, 78 of them in colour. Thames & Hudson published it in 2015.

Auerbach was born in Berlin and fled Nazi Germany as a child. Lampert directed the Whitechapel Art Gallery from 1988 to 2001 and has curated Auerbach exhibitions, including the retrospective at Tate Britain.

title: Everything She Touched: The Life of Ruth Asawa
description:
Marilyn Chase's biography of the sculptor Ruth Asawa. It begins on a California farm and ends with the hanging wire sculptures she is known for.

Asawa was a farmer's daughter who was held in a Japanese American internment camp during the Second World War. Later she raised six children in a multiracial family, founded an arts-focused high school and made public fountains in San Francisco. The book carries more than 60 reproductions of artwork and archival photographs, among them portraits by Imogen Cunningham. Chronicle Books published it in April 2020.

Asawa's sculpture is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Getty, the Whitney Museum and other institutions. The book covers the family and civic commitments that ran alongside her studio work.

title: Call Me Burroughs: A Life
description:
A full-length biography of the writer William S. Burroughs, published by Twelve in 2014 and described by its publisher as the first in 25 years.

Miles wrote with the support of the Burroughs estate and drew on interviews with Allen Ginsberg, Lucien Carr and Burroughs himself. The publisher says it is the first Burroughs biography to cover the last decade of his life and to examine his cultural legacy. The hardcover runs to 736 pages.

Barry Miles is a British writer who has documented the Beat circle and the London counterculture across several books, among them Ginsberg: A Biography, William Burroughs: El Hombre Invisible and Paul McCartney: Many Years from Now. He co-edited the Restored Text edition of Naked Lunch, and wrote the liner notes for the 1995 reissue of Burroughs's early spoken-word album, also titled Call Me Burroughs.

title: The Possible Life of Christian Boltanski
publisher: MFA Publications, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
description:
An oral autobiography of the French artist Christian Boltanski, assembled from a long interview with the art historian Catherine Grenier.

Boltanski talks through his wartime childhood, his career, his views on art and teaching, and how he made his installations. The book was published for his sixty-fifth birthday, with a foreword by Lucy Sante, and was translated from the French original, La vie possible de Christian Boltanski, by Marc Lowenthal. The clothbound volume has 242 pages and a small number of black-and-white and colour illustrations.

Boltanski (1944-2021) built installations about memory and mortality from photographs of children, worn clothing, tin boxes and light, many of them touching on Holocaust remembrance. His father survived the war in hiding, an episode he recounts in the book. Among his best-known pieces are Monument to the Lycée Chases (1986-1987) and Reserve (1989).

title: Basquiat: A Quick Killing in Art
description:
An unauthorized biography of Jean-Michel Basquiat that treats his career as a story about the 1980s art market as much as about the painter.

Hoban traces Basquiat from his Brooklyn graffiti days as SAMO to international success, his friendships with Keith Haring and Andy Warhol, and his death from an overdose in 1988 at 27. The book draws on recollections from people close to him, but his estate did not endorse it. Publishers Weekly noted that Hoban could not get permission to reproduce his work, so the 385-page text carries a few pages of plates and no paintings.

Phoebe Hoban is an American journalist. Viking issued the hardcover in August 1998 and Penguin followed with a paperback in 1999 and a revised edition in 2004.

title: Fashion Climbing: A Memoir with Photographs
description:
The memoir of the New York Times fashion photographer Bill Cunningham, found in typescript after his death and published by Penguin Press in September 2018.

His niece came upon the manuscript among his papers and photographs. It follows him from a Boston childhood in which his family disapproved of his interest in fashion, through his career as a hat designer under the name William J., to his military service in France and his decades photographing style on New York streets. Hilton Als, a friend, supplies the preface, and the book is illustrated with photographs of Cunningham himself.

Cunningham (died 2016) became known for his Times columns on street fashion and society events. The memoir covers his life through the 1960s, per Booklist, which is the period before that photographic work made him widely known.

title: The Tears of Eros
description:
A late work of art history by Georges Bataille, The Tears of Eros follows eroticism and death through the history of image-making. It was first published in French as Les larmes d'Éros in 1961, the year before his death.

The book is an illustrated essay, with notes and an index. It treats erotic art as a record of transgression, and it reproduces historical photographs of lingchi, the Chinese torture execution, which Bataille had written about since L'expérience intérieure (1943). Peter Connor translated it for City Lights Books in 1989, 213 pages in a 21 cm paperback.

Bataille (1897-1962) was a French thinker who worked across philosophy, literature, sociology and art history. He broke with the Surrealists and founded the journal Critique. His other books on these themes include Erotism and The Accursed Share, and the novel Story of the Eye.

title: A Book About Colab (and Related Activities)
description:
This book documents Collaborative Projects Inc., known as Colab, the group of young downtown New York artists who worked together from the late 1970s to the mid-1980s.

Colab made artworks, curated shows and took part in debate on the political questions of its time, and it ran projects including The Real Estate Show and The Times Square Show. The full-color book reproduces the printed matter and media the group produced and adds first-hand accounts from members. Contributing artists include Jimmy DeSana, Jenny Holzer, Kiki Smith, Liza Bear, Jane Dickson and Charlie Ahearn. It follows A Show About Colab (and Related Activities), held at Printed Matter in October and November 2011.

The editor, Max Schumann, is a former executive director of Printed Matter, the New York artists' book organization that published the volume. Printed Matter also published the 2011 show, and the book is its fullest account of Colab's output.

title: What Art Does: An Unfinished Theory
description:
In What Art Does, Brian Eno and Bette Adriaanse (credited on the cover as Bette A.) set out an "unfinished theory" of why people make and need art.

The book is richly illustrated and written in plain language. It treats art as something made by everyone, one that forms communities, opens up the world and can change the people who meet it. Faber published the hardback in January 2025, and reviewers in the Guardian and the Irish Times described it as a distillation of Eno's thinking about art.

Eno came to prominence in the early 1970s as a founding member of Roxy Music and has produced records for Talking Heads, Devo, U2 and Coldplay, among others. He is also a visual artist and has kept a published diary, A Year with Swollen Appendices. Bette A. is an Amsterdam-born artist and writer who studied Image and Language at the Gerrit Rietveld Academy.

title: Tell Them I Said No
description:
Martin Herbert's Tell Them I Said No examines artists who stepped back from the art world, whether in protest, as a deliberate conceptual act, or out of necessity.

Herbert starts from the observation that much of an artist's job in a professionalized art system is being present, and he sets retreat against that self-marketing. The ten essays cover Lutz Bacher, Stanley Brouwn, Christopher D'Arcangelo, Trisha Donnelly, David Hammons, Agnes Martin, Cady Noland, Laurie Parsons, Charlotte Posenenske and Albert York. Sternberg Press published it in November 2016, 128 pages with 25 black-and-white illustrations, designed by Fraser Muggeridge Studio.

Herbert is a Berlin-based writer and critic and an associate editor of ArtReview. His earlier books include Mark Wallinger (2011) and The Uncertainty Principle (2014).

title: The Uncertainty Principle
description:
A collection of essays on contemporary art in which not knowing, rather than mastery, is the working condition of the artist and the viewer.

Taking its title from the physics principle about the limits of measurement and the way seeing alters what is seen, the book considers art practices since the 1970s. Herbert starts from Marcel Duchamp's remark that a work is completed by the viewer, and follows artists whose works treat completion as construction. The essays move through a range of approaches to constructed experiences of not knowing, with subjects running from history and politics to epistemology and mortality. Sam de Groot designed the softcover edition.

Martin Herbert is a writer and critic who lives in Tunbridge Wells and Berlin. He is associate editor of ArtReview and contributes regularly to Artforum, frieze and Art Monthly. His earlier monograph Mark Wallinger, a study of the British artist's career, appeared in 2011.

title: Devotion
description:
A short book by Patti Smith that sets an original story beside an account of how she came to write it.

The first section is a tale of obsession involving a young skater who lives for her art, a possessive collector and a relationship built on need. The second retraces the sources of the story. Smith travels through the South of France to Camus's house, visits the garden of the publisher Gallimard, tracks down Simone Weil's grave in a cemetery outside London and walks the Paris streets of Patrick Modiano's novels. She opens her notebooks along the way. The volume runs to 112 pages with 11 black-and-white illustrations and belongs to the Why I Write series.

Smith is a National Book Award-winning author whose earlier books include Just Kids, M Train and Year of the Monkey. Devotion turns from her life story to the working life of a writer, the subject of the Why I Write series.

title: My Pinup
description:
A short two-part memoir in which Hilton Als writes about Prince and about his own longing, and about the ways love, loss, race and desire cross.

The book was published by New Directions in November 2022. Als writes toward Prince directly, addressing him in the second person, and sets his admiration beside the downtown queer nightclub scene of his youth, the AIDS crisis, Dorothy Parker and an ill-fated peach pie. The material is personal and compressed, and moves between celebrity and private life.

Als is a Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and theater critic at The New Yorker, and was earlier a staff writer at The Village Voice. His books include The Women (1996), which turns on his mother, Dorothy Dean and Owen Dodson, and White Girls (2013), essays on race, gender and identity. My Pinup runs to 48 pages.

title: On the New
description:
A philosophical study of how the new comes into being in culture, translated here into English by G. M. Goshgarian.

Groys looks at the economies of exchange and valuation that drive modern culture's key sites, the intellectual marketplace and the archive. As ideas move from one context to another, newness is created. The line separating the valuable from the worthless, and culture from profanity, keeps shifting, and that movement is the center of the investigation. The book tries to map what constitutes artistic innovation and what processes underpin its recognition and appropriation.

Boris Groys is an art critic, media theorist and philosopher, now a global distinguished professor at New York University, who works on contemporary art, Russian intellectual history and media theory. On the New translates Über das Neue: Versuch einer Kulturökonomie, published in Munich in 1992. His other books include The Total Art of Stalinism, Art Power (2008), The Communist Postscript (2010) and Introduction to Antiphilosophy (2012). Verso issued this English edition in 2014.

title: Art Lessons: Meditations on the Creative Life
description:
A book of short meditations on what it means to live as an artist, written in the tradition of Robert Henri's The Art Spirit.

Haynes addresses the mind, body and spirit of the working artist and draws on personal reflection about what it takes to make art and feel creatively and spiritually fulfilled. The lessons run from plain advice, such as keeping a pencil or crayon always to hand, to larger questions about connecting art to daily life and to the earth. Westview Press published it in Boulder in 2003 as an Icon edition, with a bibliography (pp. 185-196) and an index.

Haynes had published two academic books with Cambridge University Press before this one, which she describes as her first step toward a more personal voice. The book later went out of print. She has said it forms the core of her seventh book, Beginning Again: Reflections on Art as Spiritual Practice.

title: The War of Art: A History of Artists' Protest in America
description:
A history of artist-led activism and the political and aesthetic debates around it, from the 1960s to the present, which argues that art history is also political history.

Lauren O'Neill-Butler tells the story through studies of key individuals and artist groups and their campaigns for solidarity, housing, and LGBTQ+ and HIV/AIDS awareness. The book rests on in-depth oral histories and is illustrated throughout. Its title plays on Sun Tzu's The Art of War. Verso published the hardback in June 2025, 240 pages, and a paperback followed in June 2026.

O'Neill-Butler is a New York writer and editor, a former senior editor of Artforum and a co-founder of the nonprofit magazine November. She edits the New York art guide Vide and teaches part time at Hunter College and The New School. Her first book was Let's Have a Talk: Conversations with Women on Art and Culture (Karma, 2021).

title: On and Off-Screen Imaginaries
description:
Six essays by the artist and filmmaker Tiffany Sia that propose a framework for an exilic, fugitive cinema, written in the aftermath of the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests.

The essays take up geopolitics in cinema, image circulation and national imaginaries, and survey a new documentary vernacular produced by filmmakers who have broken from the nostalgia of Hong Kong's cinematic golden age. Sia turns to the Cold War and its afterlives, looking at ad hoc distribution networks, speculative and performative re-enactment, and countergeographic landscape imaging. Jean Ma writes the foreword. Film stills, photographs by An-my Lê and images from Sia's short film The Sojourn (2023) sit between the essays.

Sia is an artist, filmmaker and writer based in New York whose work examines how print and film trace and enable power, especially in constructing images of Hong Kong. Her short films include Never Rest/Unrest (2020), Do Not Circulate (2021) and What Rules the Invisible (2022). Earlier books are Too Salty Too Wet (Speculative Place, 2020) and Salty Wet (Inpatient Press, 2019).

title: Less Is Enough: On Architecture and Asceticism
description:
An essay that sets the idea of asceticism against modernist minimalism, arguing that today's austerity chic is a corruption of the real thing.

Aureli traces asceticism from early Christianity through medieval monasteries and examines how the monk's cell became a foundation of private property. He argues that under capitalism minimalism has been aestheticized into lifestyle branding, and he holds that a radical idea of "less" can still be recovered. A passage on Walter Benjamin's modern "barbarian", who starts from nothing and makes a little go a long way, connects the argument to minimally furnished living. Strelka Press, the publishing arm of the Strelka Institute in Moscow, released it in August 2013, first as an ebook; the paperback runs 64 pages.

Aureli is an architect and theorist who teaches at the Architectural Association in London and has been a visiting professor at Yale. His earlier books include The Project of Autonomy (2008) and The Possibility of an Absolute Architecture (2011).

title: A History of Pictures: From the Cave to the Computer Screen
description:
A two-author history of image-making that runs from prehistoric cave painting to the pictures on today's screens, written by the painter David Hockney with the critic Martin Gayford.

The book moves through painting, photography, film and digital imaging, asking how each new way of making pictures changed what people see and how they represent reality. Abrams published the US hardcover in October 2016, at 360 pages with 325 color illustrations. The cover is lettered in Hockney's own hand on a drawn blue ground.

Hockney has worked in paintings, drawings, prints, photography and digital media for more than six decades. His earlier book is Secret Knowledge: Rediscovering the Lost Techniques of the Old Masters. Gayford is an art critic whose books include Man with a Blue Scarf: On Sitting for a Portrait by Lucian Freud.

title: Rene: New York Diaries
description:
Diaries by the painter William Rand about the poet, critic and painter Rene Ricard, written in New York between 1984 and 1996.

Rand kept the entries in a shoebox in his studio. They follow East Village studio life in the 1980s and 1990s as the two men get to know each other, against street crime, drug addiction and Ricard's own fame. A reviewer notes Ricard's difficult dealings with prospective patrons, nights spent on the subway and his deep knowledge of painting. The first edition, published by Osprey Press in 2022, was a limited run of 500 copies on Mohawk Superfine, with Raymond Foye credited as a contributor. A second edition followed in 2025.

Rand is a painter, and this is his account of Ricard rather than a work of criticism. Ricard was the Artforum writer who published influential essays on Julian Schnabel and Jean-Michel Basquiat, including Radiant Child, and died in 2014 at 68.

title: Reclaiming Art in the Age of Artifice
description:
A philosophical defence of art against the media, consumer culture and artificial intelligence that Martel calls artifice.

Martel draws on examples from Paleolithic cave art to contemporary cinema. His argument is that real art discloses unseen forces shaping existence, forces that sit outside politics, technology and culture, while artifice aims to manipulate or distract its audience. Art, in his account, opens rifts onto the sublime and the weird and reconnects readers with the mystery at the centre of the world. This Basic Books edition, published in May 2025, carries an introduction by the novelist Donna Tartt and a new afterword by the author.

J.F. Martel is a writer and lecturer on art, culture and philosophy who lives in Ottawa. With the musicologist Phil Ford he hosts the art and philosophy podcast Weird Studies. The book first appeared in 2015 from North Atlantic Books under the subtitle A Treatise, Critique, and Call to Action.

title: Why Art Matters: The Bearable Lightness of Being
publisher: OCMA Books (Orange County Museum of Art)
description:
A reference guide to living with art, written by a museum director and published by her own institution.

Chapters are organised by theme, among them perseverance, the unknown, imperfection and ritual. Each entry centres on a single work of art or artist and sets out different ways to approach it, with reflections on how to bring one's best self to life. The book was issued in 2024 by OCMA Books, the Orange County Museum of Art's reestablished publishing arm, and launched at readings and signings in Laguna Beach and at the FLAG Art Foundation in New York.

Heidi Zuckerman was CEO and director of the Orange County Museum of Art. She directed the Aspen Art Museum from 2005 to 2019 and joined OCMA in 2021. She has curated more than 200 exhibitions, hosts the podcast About Art and wrote the Conversations with Artists book series.

title: The Hard Question of Art: Cognitive Futures
description:
An essay on perception as the centre of art, set against inequality, climate challenges and artificial intelligence.

Metahaven holds that art operates in the space between the image formed by the artist and the cognitive effort required to complete it. Through conceptual experiments the book follows art across cognition, empathy, complexity and physics. It asks whether aesthetic value still matters, whether art serves a moral purpose, how AI might change artistic forms, and what capacities art requires of audiences whose attention is under pressure. Verso published it in August 2026.

Metahaven is the authorial name on the cover and the only one credited on the publisher's page.

title: Anonymous Objects: Inscrutable Photographs and the Unknown
description:
An essay on photographs whose subjects cannot be named, and on what that failure shows about the limits of knowledge.

Beil argues that inscrutable photographs keep ambiguity alive: they make room for curiosity and wonder by resisting attempts to know the world by naming it. The book is a small-format paperback of 175 pages, 10 by 14.8 cm, in black and white and colour, published by SPBH Editions in September 2023 as number 5 in the SPBH Essays series and distributed with MACK.

Kim Beil is an art historian and writer based in the United States who specialises in photography and also works as a photographer and teacher.

The first 2012 issue of the F de C de Rigueur Reader, a small-format paperback edited by Alin Huma with contributions from Erik Bernhardsson, Robert Cook and Antonin Gaultier.

[sic] is the paperback reproduction of a 1993 work on paper by Sean Landers: 454 handwritten sheets of yellow lined paper, bound as a book.

Landers was born in 1962 in Palmer, Massachusetts, studied at the Philadelphia College of Art and Yale, and lives and works in New York City and Southold. title: A Giacometti Portrait
description:
James Lord's A Giacometti Portrait is a day-by-day account of sitting for Alberto Giacometti in Paris in 1964, and a record of how a single painting was begun, reworked and left unfinished.

Lord expected one or two sittings. The portrait took eighteen consecutive afternoons in September and October 1964. He transcribed Giacometti's remarks during the sessions and photographed the canvas at the end of each day, so the text follows the painting through its repeated revisions. The book first appeared in 1965. This is the Farrar, Straus and Giroux paperback of 1980, 117 pages.

Lord (1922 to 2009) was an American writer from Englewood, New Jersey, who settled in Paris after serving in the US Army in the Second World War. He later wrote Giacometti: A Biography (1985) and Picasso and Dora: A Personal Memoir (1993), and the 2017 film Final Portrait, with Armie Hammer as Lord, retells the sittings.

title: GAAG: The Guerrilla Art Action Group, 1969–1976: A Selection
contributors: Jon Hendricks (Author); Jean Toche (Author); Poppy Johnson (Author); Jan van Raay (Photography)
description:
This is the primary printed record of the Guerrilla Art Action Group, an activist artists' collective that worked from 1969 to 1976, reprinted in 2011 from the 1978 original.

The 368-page volume gathers manifestos, letters and press communiqués that the group sent to political and cultural figures. It adds facsimile documents, handwritten expense records and photographs by Ka Kwong Hui, Joanne Stamerra and others, covering 52 actions. GAAG formed in October 1969. Its members held that profit and private interest had corrupted art and culture, and they responded with symbolic, nonviolent provocation. Printed Matter first published the book in 1978. The 2011 reprint is a joint edition of Printed Matter, Kunstverein Publishing and the Research Centre for Artists' Publications at the Weserburg Museum of Modern Art.

The group's members were Jon Hendricks, Poppy Johnson, Silvianna, Joanne Stamerra, Virginia Toche and Jean Toche. The reprint credits Toche and Hendricks with Johnson, and lists Pat Steir and Paula Greif as designers and Jan van Raay as photographer.

title: Radiant: The Life and Line of Keith Haring
description:
A full-length biography of Keith Haring, written with access to the artist's archive, that follows his path from subway chalk drawings to the centre of the 1980s New York art world.

Gooch draws on that archive and on interviews with people who knew Haring to trace how he moved between street, club and gallery and between high art and popular culture. The book places him among contemporaries such as Andy Warhol and Madonna. It runs to 512 pages, and the hardcover edition appeared in 2024. The book won the 2025 Lambda Award for Biography, and a television series based on it is in production, written and directed by Andrew Haigh.

Brad Gooch is a biographer, novelist and memoirist. His earlier biographies include City Poet: The Life and Times of Frank O'Hara and Flannery: A Life of Flannery O'Connor, and he has also written the memoir Smash Cut. Radiant extends his work on twentieth-century American artists and writers to a visual artist.

title: The Esopus Reader: A Collection of Writing from Esopus, 2003-2018
description:
A single-volume selection of the writing published in Esopus, the arts and culture annual edited by Tod Lippy, across its 25 issues from 2003 to 2018.

The 448-page hardcover includes the magazine's New Voices series of fiction by never-before-published authors, several of whom later published with major imprints. Contributors write on their own working methods: the choreographer Christopher Wheeldon on ballets set to Ligeti, the lighting designer Jennifer Tipton on her discipline, and the architect Michael Arad on designing the 9/11 Memorial. Karl Ove Knausgaard writes on the value of literature. Interviews include Kenneth Lonergan, the translator Ann Goldstein and the mathematician John Conway. The book also holds poetry and theatrical monologues.

Lippy is the editor named on the Esopus Foundation's book list, which also includes Modern Artifacts (2020), co-edited with Michelle Elligott, and A Lot More Inside (2024). The foundation, incorporated in 2003, also commissions limited-edition artworks from contemporary artists.

title: How Successful Artists Study: Effective Learning Ideas and Knowledge for Artists
description:
A practical guide to an artist's education and career, written by a painter who teaches at New York art schools.

The 244-page book covers how artists prepare for criticism, work with different instructors, build confidence and collaborate. Its 18 chapters take in developing a personal style, choosing mentors, composition and colour theory, portfolio development, and what gallery dealers look for. The author presents it as a conversation with a mentor or a successful artist. It is illustrated in colour throughout.

Samuel Adoquei is a Ghanaian-born artist who has taught at the Art Students League and the National Academy School of Fine Art in New York. His work has been shown at the Smithsonian Institution and the Harvard Club, and the French town of Pomport gave him its Medal of Honor. He also wrote Origin of Inspiration and A Short Story of Skin Tones in Art.

A small book of interviews about contemporary art, written by Bill Powers and issued by the independent press Junior in an edition of 500 copies.

Early 21st Century Art measures 4.5 by 7 inches and was published in 2024. The cover carries only the title, set in black capitals at the head of a pale green wrapper. Junior describes it as a book of interviews.

Junior is an independent publishing initiative based in Cleveland, Ohio, that makes limited-edition books with artists, designers and writers. title: Widow Basquiat: A Memoir
description:
A short, intimate memoir of Jean-Michel Basquiat told from the position of Suzanne Mallouk, his girlfriend and muse, rather than from the art world's.

Clement follows Basquiat from the subways and street writing of downtown New York into the city's elite galleries. The account passes through his dealings with Madonna, Andy Warhol, Keith Haring and Julian Schnabel, and closes with his death from a heroin overdose in 1988, at twenty-seven. This Canongate edition, in its Canons series, carries an introduction by Michael Holman and an afterword by Clement. It runs to 208 pages. The book first appeared in 2000 from Payback Press.

Jennifer Clement was born in Connecticut in 1960 and raised largely in Mexico City. She also wrote novels including Prayers for the Stolen and Gun Love, and served as the first woman president of PEN International from 2015 to 2021.

title: CPLY: Reflection on a Past Life
publisher: Institute for the Arts, Rice University
description:
A small exhibition catalogue from 1979 in which the American painter William N. Copley, who signed his work CPLY, reviews his own career.

The show, held at the Rice Museum in Houston from 7 September to 11 November 1979, paired Copley's recent mirror pieces with earlier paintings and drawings drawn from Houston collections. The 39-page paperback was issued by the Institute for the Arts at Rice University and includes a works list and a lengthy essay in English by the artist. The cover reproduces a painting of a woman in a fencing mask and gloves holding a sword against a red ground.

Copley (1919-1996) was a painter, gallerist and patron. He opened the Copley Galleries in Beverly Hills in 1948, showing Magritte, Ernst, Tanguy and Man Ray, and later founded the SMS portfolios. His own work of the 1950s and 1960s mixed pin-up imagery, Western saloons and flags, and in 1974 he showed erotic work in New York as CPLY X-Rated.

author_full_name: Susan Buck-Morss, Adam Michaels, Kevin McCaughey
title: Seeing ↔ Making: Room for Thought
description:
An experimental book that treats thinking as something made from images, combining the political philosopher Susan Buck-Morss's essays with visual material arranged by the designers Adam Michaels and Kevin McCaughey.

The 400-page softcover, published by Inventory Press in 2024, calls itself a picture-book of philosophy. It draws on the ideas of Marshall McLuhan, Walter Benjamin and John Berger and uses montage and other visual techniques to explore the connection between seeing and making. Buck-Morss's pieces on visual culture, history, politics and aesthetics sit alongside the images, so that criticism and conceptual play share the page. The cover marks it as number 12 in the Innervative Spaces series.

Buck-Morss is a political theorist and Distinguished Professor of Political Science at the CUNY Graduate Center, and Professor Emerita at Cornell. Her earlier books include The Dialectics of Seeing (1989), on Benjamin's Arcades Project, Hegel, Haiti, and Universal History (2009) and Year 1: A Philosophical Recounting (2021).

title: The Use of Photography
description:
A joint book by Annie Ernaux and Marc Marie that uses photographs of a lovers' domestic aftermath to think about desire, illness and mortality.

The two met in January 2003 and became lovers almost at once, and Marie accompanied Ernaux to the Institut Curie for breast cancer surgery. They photographed the scenes left after their nights together: clothes dropped on the floor, displaced furniture, the remains of meals. The book pairs fourteen colour photographs with alternating texts by each author on love, eroticism and the changing body. Alison L. Strayer's English translation was published by Seven Stories Press in October 2024, in a 208-page paperback.

Ernaux, born in France, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2022. Her books examine class, gender and intimate experience. Marc Marie is a French journalist and photographer. According to the publisher, the project came directly before Ernaux's novel The Years.
